extracted.intended_audience: design patent applicants, patent agents, IP attorneys, and small businesses evaluating Hague System filing strategies
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance on when and how to use the WIPO Hague System for international industrial design protection and for pursuing related U.S. design patents. Covers eligibility, filing routes, drafting/formatting considerations, timing, and administrative benefits/risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement to file (eligibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: To participate in the Hague system, an applicant must show at least one entitlement to file from a member country. An entitlement can be any of: nationality, domicile, habitual residence, or real and effective industrial or commercial establishment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a client in Taiwan with a habitual residence in Japan (member country) is eligible to file through the Hague. Use entitlement rules to determine who may be the filer and which member country can be the basis for filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designation and representation rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hague design application may designate one or more Hague members. The applicant can appoint a practitioner in any Hague member country to represent them and does not need a representative for each country designated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many designs grant without ever having to appoint a local representative in the granting country; applicants can select a single practitioner in a member country (e.g., the U.S.) to handle filings and communications through WIPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: WIPO formalities vs. national substantive examination
rubrics_metrics.description: WIPO completes an examination for formalities only; after publication the application proceeds to designated offices, where substantive examination (e.g., for novelty) will be performed if required by the member country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unlike the PCT national phase, the Hague application stays with WIPO and all communication to/from designated countries passes through WIPO for the life of the application—this centralization affects prosecution workflow and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication timing control
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant can control the timing of publication (depending on which members they have designated). The standard publication now occurs at 12 months, immediate publication may be requested, or publication may be deferred by a specified number of months up to 30.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use publication timing strategically to coordinate publicity, priority filings, or market disclosure considerations for different designated countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language and cost advantages (filing in English)
rubrics_metrics.description: Centralization through WIPO allows the ability to file in English no matter which countries are designated, saving the applicant translation fees for most regions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing in English reduces translation burden and may simplify initial drafting; verify translation requirements for any designated country that requires local-language documentation after grant (if applicable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Centralized administrative management (data updates & annuities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Data updates (e.g., applicant contact information) can be handled with one notification to WIPO. Annuities for all designated countries can be handled as a single payment to WIPO and are only due every five years instead of annually for many conventional cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralized maintenance reduces administrative overhead and payment frequency, but ensure accurate centralized records to avoid lapses across multiple jurisdictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple-designs and Locarno classification rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple related U.S. designs (up to 100!) can be the subject of a single Hague filing if the designs are in the same Locarno classification (the international classification for industrial designs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group related designs into a single Hague filing where possible to save filing costs—confirm all designs fall within the same Locarno class before relying on this advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing route A — First file in the United States (then Hague priority)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a design application is filed in the United States, a priority filing can be made through the Hague within the six-month design priority window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing first in the U.S. may be appropriate when a U.S. foreign filing license is needed, when delaying publication is desirable, or when using USPTO acceleration (Rocket Docket). Conduct a pre-filing discussion about possible Hague filing within six months to plan drawings, title, descriptive language, and whether to have a foreign associate review drawings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing route B — Enter the United States through a Hague application
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hague design application can designate the United States; designating the U.S. can help control timing of examination because the USPTO must submit examination results to WIPO within 12 months of publication of the design.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO will be required to accept drawings that have passed WIPO's formalities exam (including photographs, 3D renderings, and other non-black-and-white line drawing types), but the USPTO may still issue rejections for lack of enablement. Standard restriction practice will apply during U.S. examination; deferring divisional filings until restriction can defer costs and decision points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing route C — File Hague first, then claim US priority
rubrics_metrics.description: A Hague application may be filed first (useful when imminent public exposure leaves little time to prepare a first filing); one or more U.S. applications can be filed up to six months later claiming priority to the Hague application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this route when you need immediate international filing and will later decide about U.S. prosecution or when public disclosure is imminent.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO acceptance of non-traditional drawings and enablement caveat
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO will accept drawings as long as they have passed the WIPO formalities examination (including photographs, 3D renderings, and other non-black and white line drawing types). However, the USPTO may still issue rejections for lack of enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though WIPO formalities may accept varied drawing types, practitioners should ensure that the disclosure meets USPTO enablement and statutory requirements to avoid substantive rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategic planning and complexity warning
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the Hague process strategically can open new filing options for design filers, not just for international design registration but also for their U.S. design patents. But despite its inherent benefits, the system’s complexity cannot be overlooked.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for international design registration early in the patenting process to take full advantage of Hague options; evaluate trade-offs among routes, timing, costs, and local substantive requirements with counsel or foreign associates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of eHague or office of indirect filing
rubrics_metrics.description: The application can be filed through WIPO’s eHague filing interface or through an 'office of indirect filing' (such as the USPTO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose filing channel based on practitioner preference, available local support, and whether an indirect filing office simplifies entitlement or representation requirements.
